newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX crude, products end volatile session lower.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX crude, products end volatile session lower.

text.p: Crude and oil product futures ended Wednesday's volatile NYMEX session lower across the board, with heating oil again leading the way.

The market initially moved up after mildly bullish inventory data and November crude touched its post-Gulf War high of $25.70 a barrel. But profit-taking sent crude down almost $1.00 before it recovered to end at $25.14, off 28 cents on the day.

"The market certainly was overdone (to the upside) and people were skeptical. In the absence of fresh buying it hit some voids and touched off disappointed sellers," said Steve Platt, an analyst at brokerage Dean Witter.
Heating oil futures saw the biggest swing Wednesday, dropping nearly five pct from the day's peak of 74.40 cents a gallon to the bottom at 70.75 cents before the late bounce to close at 71.40 cents.

The sharp reversal came even though the American Petroleum Institute's latest weekly report showed that heating oil inventories in the key northeast market (PADDI) fell last week, leaving them more than 18 million barrels down on their level this time last year at just 24 million barrels.

"What is spooking some people -- though the market knew about it when it went up on Monday -- is this meeting on Friday," said Gerry Samuels, an analyst at Arb Oil, referring to a gathering in Washington of oil company executives, the Energy Secretary Hazel O'Leary and a Justice Department representative to discuss what can be done to ensure that the low heating oil stocks don't hit vulnerable consumers too hard in the event of a severe winter.

Though the Energy Department is on record several times over the past few months saying it will not intervene in the market, there has been persistant speculation among market participants that companies may agree to take voluntary action.
Exxon Corp, for example, is rumored to have told clients that it will stop or at least curtail exports of distillates if the situation continues, though the company declines to comment.
But some other market participants reckon the market is just showing classic signs of fatigue after a long bull run.
"Any time the market doesn't react the way it should to bullish news tells me two things: It is long and the bears are in control," said Jack McIntyre, an analyst at MCM.
The volatility also is symptomatic of the later stages of a bull run, though analysts generally are not calling an end to the bullish phase.

"If you are a chartist and you step back from today and look at the market, nothing really looks that bad on the charts," said Samuels of Arb Oil. "We've had a substantial three-month bull trend and there is a bit of give-back going on."
